newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Delayed Italian entry to EMU being considered.
newsitem.headline: Delayed Italian entry to EMU being considered.

text.p: European Union officials said on Wednesday that a compromise plan delaying Italy's membership of a monetary union into the next century is under consideration by certain governments.
"I can't confirm to which extent this is something which has been completely worked out, but in some quarters people are definitely thinking about this," a senior EU official said.

The Financial Times reported on Wednesday that Italy will be offered a deal which would delay its entry into economic and monetary union until 2000 or 2001. The single currency is due to begin in 1999.
Senior Italian Treasury officials told Reuters they were unaware of such a plan and would not consider late entry into EMU.

Without specifically naming which countries might be considering the delay option, EU sources said it was among those "which have an interest to start (EMU) with a hard core of countries," a clear reference to Germany.

Officials also said such an option had to be realistic and credible and would likely be spelled out in more detail ahead of early 1998 when the EU will decide on which countries qualify for the common currency.
They cautioned, however, that such a plan is not on the agenda of the EU's monetary committee, comprised of national treasury and central bank officials, or of any other official grouping.

The problem of EMU latecomers has to be dealt with over the next several months, but officially the focus will be more on the technical aspects rather than compromise plans for those unlikely to meet the Maastricht criteria.
"The second-waver arrangement certainly doesn't include any guarantees for Italy," said another monetary official.
He added that any thinking about delayed entry for Italy or others would only be discussed privately and within national capitals.

Balancing the desires of countries like Italy, which wants desperately to be among the founding members of a single currency, and the need to ensure a credible launch to monetary union is a problem which has recently come into sharper focus.
Central to the problem is a proper definition of sustainable economic convergence, an issue close to heart of Germany.
While Italy has made great strides in meeting the economic conditions for EMU entry, there are doubts whether its efforts are durable.
Officials fear Italian membership of monetary union in the first wave might undermine the single currency in its fragile early stage.
Officials warned that talk of delayed entry at this stage could undermine investor confidence and lead to increased turbulence on currency and bond markets.
Still, they acknowledged that some resolution to the dilemma would have to be found in advance of next year's decision on which countries qualify.
"What they don't want is a big split," said another official. "I think they will make a big effort to clarify all the issues beforehand."
